In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring/io-wq: save worker type before dropping its reference

io_wq_cancel_tw_create() inspects cb->func after calling
io_worker_cancel_cb(). For an existing worker, that call can drop the
last worker reference and wake io_worker_exit(). If the canceling task
is preempted, the worker can be unlinked and freed by kfree_rcu() before
the callback function is inspected. KASAN reports a slab-use-after-free
read in this path.

Save whether the callback belongs to an unpublished continuation worker
while its reference is still held, then use the saved result for the
conditional free. This preserves the existing accounting and frees only
the worker allocated for the canceled continuation.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring/net: mask socket type with SOCK_TYPE_MASK in io_socket_bpf_populate()

When an IORING_OP_SOCKET request is prepared in io_socket_prep(),
sock->type retains creation flags such as SOCK_CLOEXEC and SOCK_NONBLOCK
until __sys_socket_file() masks them off with SOCK_TYPE_MASK during
execution.

However, io_socket_bpf_populate() copies sock->type into
bctx->socket.type without masking off ~SOCK_TYPE_MASK. As a result, a
cBPF filter inspecting bctx->socket.type against socket types such as
SOCK_DGRAM or SOCK_STREAM can be bypassed by ORing SOCK_CLOEXEC or
SOCK_NONBLOCK into the socket type.

Mask sock->type with SOCK_TYPE_MASK when populating bctx->socket.type.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring/register: enforce per-task restrictions in io_uring_register_blind()

When io_uring_register(2) is invoked with fd == -1, it dispatches
directly to io_uring_register_blind() without checking
current->io_uring_restrict.

As a result, a task with per-task register restrictions installed via
IORING_REGISTER_RESTRICTIONS can still invoke blind registration opcodes
such as IORING_REGISTER_SEND_MSG_RING even when those opcodes are not in
the task's allowed register_op bitmap.

Check current->io_uring_restrict->register_op in
io_uring_register_blind() before dispatching blind registration opcodes.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring/bpf-ops: clear bpf_ctx while submitting SQEs

bpf_io_uring_submit_sqes() calls io_submit_sqes() from inside the loop
program, with current->bpf_ctx set, and requests issued inline run with
it set too. The socket code uses has_current_bpf_ctx() to recognize
calls from bpf_setsockopt() and friends, where the caller holds the
socket lock and has already been vetted, and skips both.

So a SOCKET_URING_OP_SETSOCKOPT from the SQ passes sockopt_capable()
without the capability, and runs without lock_sock(). A task with no
capability can set SO_MARK, IP_TRANSPARENT or TCP_REPAIR, and two
threads changing IP_OPTIONS on one socket, one through the ring, double
free in no time. SOCK_DESTROY via IORING_OP_SENDMSG ends up in
tcp_abort() without the lock the same way.

Clear the run context around io_submit_sqes(). The SQEs come from
userspace and must be issued like those of any other ring. They still
run inside the program's RCU tasks trace read section, so a request
that sleeps there holds up that grace period, but other request types
do that already.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring: free the task context after a grace period

A task other than the owner can free a request, io_ring_exit_work()
running the local task_work of a DEFER_TASKRUN ring for example, or
io_do_iopoll() reaping completions. io_put_task() then takes the else
branch:

    percpu_counter_sub(&tctx->inflight, 1);
    if (unlikely(atomic_read(&tctx->in_cancel)))
            wake_up(&tctx->wait);
    put_task_struct(tctx->task);

The first line is what lets the owner leave io_uring_cancel_generic(),
and on exec it frees the tctx right after. Nothing holds that off for
the remaining three lines, the task reference only covers a tctx freed
along with the task_struct. It used to work out because
io_uring_del_tctx_node() took the uring_lock that the freeing side holds
across io_put_task(), until that moved to tctx_lock.

Free the tctx with kfree_rcu(), and enter an RCU read section in
io_put_task() before the count is dropped.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring/sqpoll: don't wait for the thread to exit

io_sq_thread_stop() wakes the SQPOLL thread and waits for it to exit.
The thread belongs to the thread group that created the ring, so a
SIGSTOP or the cgroup freezer holds it in get_signal(), and the wake up
doesn't change that. io_ring_exit_work() then sleeps in that wait until
someone continues or kills the process. iou_exit has 64 slots, so 64
closed SQPOLL rings of a stopped process keep every other ring from
being freed, for everyone.

Don't wait. Set the stop bit, wake the thread, and let it exit when it
gets to run again. The sqd can now outlive its last ring, so give it a
second refcount with one reference for the rings and one for the thread,
and free it with the last one. The thread can't reach a freed ring,
rings leave ctx_list before dropping their reference, and the io-wq hash
is refcounted.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring: defer foreign io-wq enqueues to task_work

An IOPOLL ring without DEFER_TASKRUN can be reaped by a task other than
the one that submitted the I/O. If a polled request is marked
REQ_F_REISSUE, io_free_batch_list() calls io_queue_iowq() with the
original tctx. Ordinary task exit can tear down tctx->io_wq after
draining only the tracked requests. The live request pins the task, but
not its io-wq, so the foreign task can race io_wq_put_and_exit() and
enqueue through a freed or NULL queue.

Forward foreign userspace enqueues to the owning task before accessing
tctx->io_wq. Use a dedicated task_work callback so reissues still go
straight to io-wq, and fail them if task_work is running in cancellation
mode. Preserve the existing PF_KTHREAD cancellation path. This also
covers the other callers of io_queue_iowq() without changing the
worker-owned enqueue path.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring/cancel: drop sqd->lock while SQPOLL waits

An exiting SQPOLL thread calls io_uring_cancel_generic() with sqd->lock
held, and keeps it across cond_resched() and the sleep until nothing is
in flight anymore. A zero-copy send notification can't be canceled and
stays pending as long as the peer doesn't read, so the lock is held for
as long as a user cares to. io_ring_exit_work() needs it to park the
thread, and so do IORING_REGISTER_IOWQ_AFF and IOWQ_MAX_WORKERS. With
64 such rings sharing the thread, every iou_exit slot sleeps on the lock
and no ring gets freed for anyone.

Drop the lock around cond_resched() and the sleep, like the main loop of
the thread does. Each walk of ctx_list is still under one hold, and
nothing is kept across the unlock. The thread drops its io-wq, frees its
tctx and clears sqd->thread under one hold after the loop, so whoever
holds the lock and finds sqd->thread set can still use them.

[axboe: adapted to the schedule_timeout() based loop]

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

io_uring/poll: cancel all matching requests in one pass

With IORING_ASYNC_CANCEL_ALL, __io_async_cancel() calls io_try_cancel()
until nothing is found, and io_poll_cancel() cancels one request per
call, starting each lookup at the beginning of the hash. A cancelled
request stays hashed until its task work runs, so every lookup walks
past the ones already cancelled. Cancelling K of N pending polls visits
about K*N/2 requests in one io_uring_enter(), with uring_lock held.

A single CANCEL_FD|ALL on 80000 polls on one eventfd takes 17.06s,
0.02s with this change. With voluntary preemption the soft lockup
watchdog fires:

  watchdog: BUG: soft lockup - CPU#1 stuck for 26s! [repro:100]
  RIP: 0010:io_cancel_req_match+0x19/0xa0
   io_poll_cancel+0x73/0x170
   io_try_cancel+0x7b/0xf0
   __io_async_cancel+0x41/0x110

Walk the hash once and cancel every match, as io_cancel_remove() does
for futex and waitid. Cancel by user_data only needs its own bucket.
__io_async_cancel() still loops until nothing is found, so a request
that io-wq parks in the poll hash meanwhile is still cancelled.

A cancel that matches one request now walks the whole hash twice instead
of stopping at the match.

The main hackney.erl module has maybe_strip_auth_on_redirect/2 (guarded by the location_trusted option) to address CVE-2018-1000007, but hackney_h3.erl is missing this protection entirely.

Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling vulnerability in benoitc hackney allows Flooding.

The URL parser in src/hackney_url.erl converts every unrecognized URL scheme to a permanent BEAM atom via binary_to_atom/2. BEAM atoms are never garbage-collected and the atom table defaults to a hard limit of 1,048,576 entries. An attacker who can supply URLs with attacker-chosen scheme prefixes — directly as request targets, as configured webhook URLs, or via Location headers followed during redirects — can exhaust the atom table and crash the entire BEAM VM with system_limit.

This issue affects hackney: from 2.0.0 before 4.0.1.

Flowintel's community data launcher script passes the admin API key as a command-line argument to a child Python helper process. On Unix-like systems, process arguments are readable by all local users via standard tools such as ps or by reading /proc/<pid>/cmdline, allowing any local user to observe the key while the helper process is running.

An attacker with local access to the host can capture the admin API key during the brief window in which the helper process is active. Possession of the key grants full administrative access to the Flowintel REST API, enabling unauthorized creation, modification, or deletion of threat intelligence data, users, roles, and organisations.

Preconditions:
- The victim must invoke the community data import or deletion command (launch.sh -tdc or -dtdc) with the API key supplied as a positional argument.
- The attacker must have a local user account on the same host and be able to observe process listings during the helper execution window.

Impact:
- Disclosure of the Flowintel admin API key to any local user.
- Subsequent full administrative control over the Flowintel instance via its REST API.

Affected: <4.1.0

items.summary: vulnerability-lookup prior to version 7.1.0 contains two security issues in its web interface. First, the /user/toggle_2fa endpoint accepted HTTP GET requests and disabled the authenticated user's two-factor authentication without requiring password confirmation. Because the state-changing operation was reachable via GET, an attacker with a basic account could embed an image element (or any other GET-triggering markup) in a comment pointing to that endpoint. When a victim with 2FA enabled viewed the comment, their browser silently issued the GET request, disabling the victim's second factor of authentication. No CSRF token was enforced on the GET path, and no password was required to confirm the action. Second, the comment detail page (/comment/<uuid>) rendered unpublished comments to any visitor who possessed the URL, bypassing the moderation workflow that was intended to keep such content hidden until approved. The API correctly restricted access, but the web view did not enforce the same authorization check. The combined effect allows an attacker to degrade a victim's account security (removal of 2FA) through a single page view and to read content that was not yet approved for public release.

Validating an untrusted URL with a long scheme and many hosts into a multi-host URL field (e.g. PostgresDsn) takes quadratic time and memory: an input of about a hundred kilobytes takes around a gigabyte of memory to validate.

The parse_multihost_url() function (in pydantic-core/src/validators/url.rs) parses each host separately, prepending the whole URL prefix (including the scheme) to every one of them. As the scheme can be arbitrarily long, and is parsed and stored once per host, both time and memory grow quadratically with the input size. Allowed schemes (e.g. postgres for PostgresDsn) are only checked after parsing, so they don't prevent the issue.

The issue was fixed in commit b4028f9d87e34750e53be0ba011d70f3c0fcc94e.

Impact: denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted strings into multi-host URL fields (PostgresDsn, MongoDsn, NatsDsn, or custom types built on MultiHostUrl).

Validating an untrusted string in exponent notation into a Fraction field computes the full power of ten without any bound: an input of a few bytes takes seconds to validate.

String inputs are passed to the Fraction constructor. For strings in exponent notation (e.g. '1e8000000'), CPython computes the corresponding power of ten as an integer (in Lib/fractions.py).

The issue was fixed in commit 69ed168e9ad465eef4c8d81efb152a93b604daf5. For strings in exponent notation, the exponent is now parsed before calling the Fraction constructor, and exponents larger than 4300 (in absolute value) are rejected.

Impact: denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted strings into Fraction fields (in both JSON and Python mode, including in strict mode), using Pydantic from 2.10.0 up to (but excluding) 2.14.0.

From 2.14.0, exponents larger than 4300 (in absolute value) are rejected, matching the maximum number of digits accepted for integers.

When extra data is allowed, providing both the alias and the name of an aliased TypedDict or dataclass field makes the unvalidated value (provided under the name) overwrite the validated one (provided under the alias), resulting in validated data not matching the declared type.

Extra items are stored in the same dictionary as the fields (the returned dictionary for TypedDict, the instance __dict__ for dataclasses). As only the alias is marked as used, the field name is treated as an extra item, and its unvalidated value overrides the validated one. Impact: denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted lists into fields constrained with unique_items=True (using conlist() or Field()).

The fix only applies to lists of builtin scalar types (int, float, str, bytes, bool and None), for which duplicates can be detected in linear time. Validating an untrusted ISO 8601 duration string into a timedelta field with Pydantic V1 takes quadratic time: an input of a few dozen kilobytes takes seconds to validate.

The issue was fixed in commit 62791e66a9f8f118e465ed760c9e2ede9ae3055e. Users relying on the pydantic.v1 namespace in Pydantic V2 should upgrade to 2.14.2 or later.

Impact: denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted strings into timedelta fields.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ASoC: amd: ps: fix snd_acp63_remove() teardown ordering

The ACP IRQ handlers dereference the SoundWire, SoundWire DMA, and PDM
child platform devices, but snd_acp63_remove() unregisters them while
the interrupt is still held by devres, which frees it only after remove
returns. An interrupt in this window is a use-after-free.

Mask the ACP interrupt sources and call devm_free_irq() before the
first child device is unregistered. The masking goes through the new
acp_hw_ops->disable_interrupts callback, keeping the remove path
platform-agnostic. The interrupt line is shared, and acp_hw_deinit()
clears the sources only after the children are gone, which would
leave the line raised with no handler left to ack it. The window

Loop with Unreachable Exit Condition ('Infinite Loop') vulnerability in benoitc hackney allows Excessive Allocation.

The Alt-Svc response header parser in src/hackney_altsvc.erl does not guarantee forward progress. When parse_token/2 receives a non-token, non-whitespace, non-comma byte (e.g. !, @, =, ;), it returns the input unchanged. skip_comma/1 also returns the buffer unchanged when the first byte is not a comma. parse_entries/2 then recurses with identical data, creating a tight infinite tail-recursive loop that pins a scheduler at 100% CPU. The calling process never returns.

The entry point parse_and_cache/3 is called synchronously in the connection process on every HTTP response. A single-byte Alt-Svc: ! response header is sufficient to trigger the hang; the header is fully controlled by any HTTP origin the client connects to.

This issue affects hackney: from 2.0.0-beta.1 before 4.0.1.

Unexpected Status Code or Return Value vulnerability in ninenines gun (gun_http module) allows a malicious HTTP server to force the client into raw protocol mode via an unsolicited 101 Switching Protocols response.

In gun_http:handle_inform/8, when a 101 Switching Protocols response is received over HTTP/1.1, the function verifies only that the Upgrade header is syntactically valid and that the stream reference is a plain reference(). It does not check whether the client ever sent an Upgrade or Connection: upgrade header on the corresponding request. Because this check is absent, any 101 response (solicited or not) causes gun to dispatch a gun_upgrade message to the caller and transition the entire connection to raw protocol mode.

A malicious or compromised HTTP server can send an unsolicited 101 response to any HTTP/1.1 request, causing the gun client to abandon HTTP framing for that connection. Once in raw mode, gun_raw applies no flow control (flow=infinity) and re-arms socket active mode after every received packet, so the server can flood the client with arbitrary bytes. These are forwarded as unbounded gun_data messages to the owner process, exhausting its mailbox and BEAM memory, ultimately crashing the VM.

This issue affects gun: from 2.0.0-pre.1 before 2.4.0.

items.summary:
Uncontrolled Resource Consumption vulnerability in ninenines gun (gun_http module) allows a malicious server to exhaust client memory via unbounded HTTP/1.1 response buffering.

In gun_http:handle/5, three clauses accumulate incoming TCP data into the connection's buffer field using binary concatenation with no upper-bound check: the head clause appends data until the \r\n\r\n header terminator is found; the body_chunked clause appends data whenever cow_http_te:stream_chunked/2 returns a more result indicating an incomplete chunk boundary; and the body_trailer clause appends data until the trailing \r\n\r\n is found. In each case, when the expected terminator never arrives, the enlarged binary is stored back into state and the process waits for more data, with no configurable or hard-coded ceiling on buffer size.

A malicious or compromised server can exploit this by sending a partial response that never completes. For example, a response may begin with HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nX-Pad:  followed by an unbounded stream of arbitrary bytes, never sending the header terminator. The gun connection process will continuously append the incoming data to its buffer, causing unbounded heap growth. Because BEAM imposes no per-process heap limit by default, a single malicious connection can exhaust all available memory on the node, causing a node-wide out-of-memory crash.

This issue affects gun: from 1.0.0-pre.1 before 2.4.0.

Origin Validation Error vulnerability in ninenines gun (gun_http2 module) allows cross-origin cookie injection via unvalidated HTTP/2 PUSH_PROMISE authority.

In gun_http2:push_promise_frame/7, the :authority pseudo-header from an incoming PUSH_PROMISE frame is stored verbatim into the promised stream record without checking that it matches the connection's origin. When gun_http2:headers_frame/9 later processes the response headers for the promised stream, it calls gun_cookies:set_cookie_header/7 with the unvalidated server-supplied authority before any status branching and before user code can act. This violates RFC 7540 §10.6 / RFC 9113 §8.4, which require receivers to treat as a protocol error any push for a resource the server is not authoritative for.

A malicious or compromised HTTP/2 server can plant cookies scoped to arbitrary third-party domains into the client's shared cookie store. This enables session fixation attacks against those domains and, if the planted cookie overrides a legitimate session token, may result in account takeover. No user interaction beyond making a normal HTTP/2 request to the attacker-controlled server is required.

This issue affects gun: from 2.0.0-pre.2 before 2.4.0.
